A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching authors, methods and experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison. V1 contains Appendices A–J; v2 retains these and adds Appendix K.

before.justification: V1 reports original adapter-training experiments, SAE feature-label evaluations, topic retrieval, model-scaling results and bridge-entity detection, together with appendix ablations.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and reports revised SAE evaluations, new LoRA and linear-probe comparisons, and additional label-disagreement analyses.

M1.justification: The frozen language model, adapter architectures, normalization, cross-entropy objective, layer-0 injection and multiscale generation remain unchanged. New inference explanations document existing operations; independent rescoring changes evaluation rather than the proposed adapter.

E1.justification: Both versions cover Goodfire, Llama Scope and Gemma Scope SAE features, Wikipedia contrastive topics and TwoHopFact bridge entities. New comparisons and diagnostic analyses reuse this coverage. Adding detection F1 at 70B extends evaluation of the retained SAE-labeling task.

E2.justification: V2 adds two substantively different trained comparator families: rank-4 LoRA Activation Oracles on Wikipedia and Goodfire evaluations, and layer-specific linear probes trained with InfoNCE for bridge-entity detection (Sections 3.4 and 3.6). Existing baselines are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix A.5 replaces direct best-of-six SAE score reporting with candidate selection followed by independent rescoring, affecting Tables 2, 3 and 11 and Appendix I. V2 also adds 70B detection scoring using a 70B judge and Goodfire activation contexts, and a matched 1,000-latent ALL-CAPS comparison. Coverage and Wikipedia retrieval retain their earlier reporting protocols.

E4.justification: New Appendix K investigates disagreement between detection-optimal and generation-optimal labels, presenting five extreme cases per 70B adapter and scale analyses of the top twenty. Appendix I revises the format-versus-semantics analysis with matched rescoring and format-selection measurements, replacing the earlier four-lowest-scales comparison. Figure 7 also revises the training-data-size results; most existing ablations remain.

E5.justification: Independent selection and reporting seeds replace selection-biased maxima for the principal stochastic SAE metrics, substantially changing statistical estimation. Table 11 and the revised ALL-CAPS comparison newly report uncertainty estimates. Existing SEM, confidence-interval and paired-test practices remain; the changes do not establish additional training-seed replications.

E6.justification: Many SAE scores are replaced under the revised protocol. In Table 3, SA changes from 71.4% to 66.8% hit rate and SA+LR from 68.3% to 69.7%, reversing their ranking. The abstract's 71% versus 63% comparison corresponds to SA versus paraphrases, whereas 70% versus 50% corresponds to SA+LR versus repeated original labels. These are not comparable performance gains across versions. V2 also adds 70B F1, comparator and disagreement results, and revises Figure 7 and ALL-CAPS findings.

T1.justification: Appendix K newly defines a disagreement statistic combining detection-F1 and generation-hit-rate gaps between the two selected labels. This limited mathematical addition supports example ranking; the adapter mathematics remains unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contributions: lightweight adapters trained on interpretability artifacts improve frozen-model self-interpretation, transfer across settings and recover implicit bridge entities, with favorable scaling. Revised headline comparisons change the supporting evidence and emphasis, rather than these core capability claims.

C2.justification: Appendix K introduces a core-versus-periphery interpretation of why detection and generation prefer different labels and scales, and argues for multiple candidate descriptions. Section 3.4 explicitly discusses metric-dependent architecture tradeoffs. Appendix A.5 and Table 8 newly explain selection bias and limitations on comparing results produced by different scoring protocols.

D1.justification: V2 supplies additional scoring details, including Table 8's four-scale, one-trial procedure, Table 11's sample count and rescoring trials, and the 70B detection judge and activation-cache source. Appendix K provides adapter-specific grids and latent lookup instructions. Training hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain, but v1's explicit code-and-trained-adapter release statement and link are removed.

R1.justification: The bibliography is unchanged. However, v2 newly positions frozen adapters as empirically competitive with Activation Oracles and contrasts their free-form descriptions with fixed-entity linear probes. The broader positioning as complementary to language-model fine-tuning remains.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten, methods gain dedicated inference and evaluation subsections, and the experimental narrative is reorganized around architecture and geometry before cross-dataset evaluation and scaling. Explanations are expanded throughout the main text, and Appendix K adds a substantial new discussion.

P2.justification: Table 3 gains a detection-F1 column, Table 18 adds paired-label examples, and Figure 7 is redrawn with revised vertical ranges. Several captions expand and figures and tables move with the reorganized text. Most displays and the overall two-column design are retained.

improvement.justification: V1 reports maxima from noisy candidate scores; v2 independently rescores selected labels, addressing a material source of inflation in the central SAE evidence. The new trained baselines and explicit analysis of metric-dependent labels further strengthen assessment of the method. Removal of the code/adapters link and retention of older protocols for coverage and cross-layer results are drawbacks, but the substantial improvement in evaluation reliability outweighs them.
